Issues.Title: Migrate FabricBot Tasks to Config-as-Code
Issues.Body:
**TL;DR;** Requesting to add [FabricBot](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/fabricbot_overview) configuration associated with your repository to `.github/fabricbot.json`.

**Context**

FabricBot is now a [config-as-code-only](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/bot-config-as-code) platform. As a result, while you can still use the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/coreclr) to modify your FabricBot configuration, you can no longer save the changes. The only way to save changes to your configuration at the moment is to _export configuration_ from the portal and upload the exported configuration to `.github/fabricbot.json` in your repository. In this pull request, we are adding your FabricBot configuration to your repository at `.github/fabricbot.json` so that you can make changes to it going forward.

While the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/coreclr) is the *only way* to modify your FabricBot configuration at the moment, we have a feature on our backlog to publish the JSON schema defining the structure of the FabricBot configuration file. With the JSON schema, you can (1) use a plaintext editor of your choice to modify the FabricBot configuration file and use the schema to validate the file after editing or (2) [configure](https://code.visualstudio.com/Docs/languages/json#_json-schemas-and-settings) VS Code to use the schema when editing FabricBot configuration file to take advantage of convenience features such as automatic code completion and field description on mouseover.

[*Pull Request Create*](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/prcreate), a [MerlinBot](https://https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot) Extension, was used to automatically create this pull request. If you have any questions or concerns with this pull request, please contact [MerlinBot Expert DRI](mailto:merlinbotdri@microsoft.com).

Issues.Title: Confusing behavior when using AssemblyInfo.cs
Issues.Body:
I'm completely perplexed.

I created a .Net Standard 2.0 library project.

I explicity added an AssemblyInfo.cs file, we need this because we use this utility to "stamp" our assemblies when we build them:

https://github.com/ygoe/NetRevisionTool

That utility is run as a pre/post build event and temporarily replaces placeholders in the AssemblyInformationalVersion attribute with runtime values (like repo folder name, commit ID, branch etc etc).

The completed assembly then has this info "burned" into it as we go forward.

.Net Standard is not working with this.

2. The version of the generated nuget package is always set as 1.0.0.

This is just mind blowing, is there no way we can do this seemingly simple operation any more if adopt .Net Standard?

Issues.Title: Questions about tagging within this repository / future versions
Issues.Body:
I was looking through this repository to determine if .NET Standard 2.1 libraries support default interface methods - it looks like they do, given the presence of `System.Runtime.CompilerServices.RuntimeFeature.DefaultImplementationsOfInterfaces`, as well as my own experimenting in VS 2019. It seems I was mistaken when thinking that this was not the case, so I'm glad this repository is easily accessible to determine this.

But while doing this, I found it difficult to determine what commits were included in this particular .NET Standard version. I see that there's a tag `v2.1.0-prerelease.19126.1`, as well as branches `release/2.0.0`, `release/3.0`, and `release/3.0-preview9`. One of the machines I tested VS 2019 on had a `netstandard.dll` assembly, itself targeting .NETStandard v2.1.0, with AssemblyInformationalVersion `1.1.0+a5b5f2e1e369972c8ff1e2183979fab6099f52ef`; this commit is part of the `release/3.0` branch. However, another machine had a same-named assembly, targeting .NETCoreApp v3.0 and AssemblyInformationalVersion `3.0.0+4ac4c0367003fe3973a3648eb0715ddb0e3bbcea`, and I don't see that commit hash in this repository.

Additionally, [this blog post](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/the-future-of-net-standard/) states that 2.1 will be the last version, but there is another prerelease tag `v2.2.0-prerelease.19564.1` and [on GitHub](https://github.com/dotnet/standard/releases/tag/v2.2.0-prerelease.19564.1) it's labelled .NET 5.0 Preview 2.

So I have a few questions for understanding this repository:

1. Since .NET Standard 2.1 is released, are there plans to continue development in this repository for e.g. the shared BCL going forward with .NET 5+?
2. Are there multiple kinds of `netstandard.dll` for a single .NET Standard version? E.g. are there separate versions for .NET Framework to reference and for .NET Core / .NET 5+ to reference?
3. Do the tags / branch names in this repository correspond to a .NET Standard version or something else?
4. It looks like there are patch releases; are there patch versions of a single .NET Standard version?
5. Are there other repositories which are being used to create `netstandard.dll`?
6. Is there a way to determine, from the repository, which commit is the one used for a given release?

Thank you for your consideration.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Questions about tagging within this repository / future versions" (#1777)

Issues.Title: Issue with resolving between .NET Standard 2.0 and .NET Standard 2.1
Issues.Body:
# Summary

.NET Standard version is not resolved correctly when a transitive dependency targets multiple .NET Standard versions.

# Environment

- Windows 10 (19042.746)
- .NET 5 SDK 5.0.201

# Minimal reproducible example
[bug.zip](https://github.com/dotnet/standard/files/6209239/bug.zip)

This is a three-project solution:
- `TestProject1` targeting `netcoreapp3.1`
- `ClassProject1` targeting `netstandard2.0`
- `ClassProject2` targeting *both* `netstandard2.0` and `netstandard2.1`

The project dependency chain is: `TestProject1 -> ClassProject1 -> ClassProject2`

A method (`ClassProject2Test1`) on `ClassProject2` is hidden behind a `#if NETSTANDARD2_0` preprocessor directive.

# The issue

The unit test failed with a `MissingMethodException`

```
[xUnit.net 00:00:00.38]     TestProject1.UnitTest1.Test1 [FAIL]
  Failed TestProject1.UnitTest1.Test1 [2 ms]
  Error Message:
   System.MissingMethodException : Method not found: 'Void ClassLibrary2.Class2.Class2Test1()'.
  Stack Trace:
     at ClassLibrary1.Class1.Class1Test1()
   at TestProject1.UnitTest1.Test1() in C:\Users\rex\source\netstandard-bug-repro\TestProject1\UnitTest1.cs:line 12
```

# Expected result

The compiler should have resolved the chain as:

`TestProject1 (.NET Core 3.1) -> ClassProject1 (.NET Standard 2.0) -> *ClassProject2 (.NET Standard 2.0)*` 

# Actual result

The compiler resolved the chain as:

`TestProject1 (.NET Core 3.1) -> ClassProject1 (.NET Standard 2.0) -> *ClassProject2 (.NET Standard 2.1)*` 

Which causes the exception because the offending method, `ClassProject2Test1`, was hidden by the `#if NETSTANDARD2_0` preprocessor directive.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Issue with resolving between .NET Standard 2.0 and .NET Standard 2.1" (#1787)

Issues.Title: Security Vulnerability due to System.Text.RegularExpressions
Issues.Body:
### Problem
There is a security vulnerability with the version of System.Text.RegularExpressions that is used by dotnet standard. The vulnerable version of System.Text.RegularExpressions is 4.3.0. Please see links below for the vulnerability documentation or discussion:

https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/en-US/vulnerability/CVE-2019-0820
https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/111
https://cve.mitre.org/cgi-bin/cvename.cgi?name=CVE-2019-0820
https://snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-DOTNET-SYSTEMTEXTREGULAREXPRESSIONS-174708
https://www.whitesourcesoftware.com/vulnerability-database/CVE-2019-0820

The dotnet commit that fixed the vulnerability is https://github.com/dotnet/corefx/commit/19d4b1163d8a03dd90ff5fd1785eea6305112545

### Issue:
We use whitesource and it has caught this issue with high severity. We don't consume System.Text.RegularExpressions directly but packages that use this. Therefore as a transitive dependency due to NetStandard library, which is being used by several other dotnet packages like Castle Windsor, MassTransit etc., Once an update is available the others could followup and update.

### Code:

[The latest version 2.0.3 of Net standard ](https://www.nuget.org/packages/NETStandard.Library/) still seem to be using System.Text.RegularExpressions version 4.3.0 as per https://github.com/dotnet/standard/blob/master/src/apicompat/netstandard/netstandard.depproj

### Fix
Please update[ library](https://www.nuget.org/packages/NETStandard.Library/) targeting .netStandard 1.6 to update System.Text.RegularExpression package to latest secured version 4.3.1 to fix the security issue or kindly suggest alternatives.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Security Vulnerability due to System.Text.RegularExpressions" (#1786)

Issues.Title: linq using GetValueOrDefault  in Where clause problem
Issues.Body:
Hello,

I am currently using .NET core 2.2.x and EF Core. 2.2.6. I have a function that returns a List<Animal> from the database with no issue. It returns 11 results. However, when I try to use `.Where(p => p.DeletedAt.GetValueOrDefault(DateTime.Now) => DateTime.Now).ToList()`, it still should return 11 results, however it returns 0. I also eliminated the possibility that there is something wrong with my where clause (logic) because it works perfectly on 4.6.1 EF Core 2.2.6. Furthermore, I confirmed that it is only where I am comparing a nullable type using that function and I am guessing that I missed a thread someone opened on this issue. I am aware .NET core 2.2 is not LTS. I also thought this goes here because it's not AFAIK, an EF core issue but rather an Ienumerable/Linq issue.

Update: As it turns out your notion of `DateTime.Now` getting evaluated twice is true. To rectify that, I will now be using `DateTime.Now.Date`. This is odd because this exact code works on 4.6.1. You're probably right. SMH. Thank you @GrabYourPitchforks! You may now close.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "linq using GetValueOrDefault  in Where clause problem" (#1792)

Issues.Title: Strong name signature not valid
Issues.Body:
Since I've ported a ClickOnce application from .NET Framework 4.6.1 to .NET Standard 2.0, the message _"Strong assembly name signature not valid for **Microsoft.SqlServer.Assessment.Types.dll**"_ appears when trying to install or update the application. So the next step was to verify the assembly strong name by using the [Strong Name Tool](https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/framework/tools/sn-exe-strong-name-tool) to make sure, that everything is fine, but:

```sh
> sn.exe -v Microsoft.SqlServer.Assessment.Types.dll

Microsoft (R) .NET Framework Strong Name Utility Version 4.0.30319.0
Copyright (c) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.

Microsoft.SqlServer.Assessment.Types.dll is a delay-signed or test-signed assembly
```

Additional information:

- The assembly versions `161.46041.41` and `161.46367.54` ended up in the same result
- This issue looks very similar to [this](https://www.damirscorner.com/blog/posts/20140502-StrongNameValidationFailedSecurityException.html)
- @markingmyname / @olprod: The root package, which is required for [Server Management Objects (SMOs)](https://docs.microsoft.com/sql/relational-databases/server-management-objects-smo/overview-smo?view=sql-server-ver15), is:
  - [Microsoft.SqlServer.SqlManagementObjects](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.SqlServer.SqlManagementObjects)
    - Microsoft.SqlServer.Assessment
      - Microsoft.SqlServer.Assessment.Authoring
        - **Microsoft.SqlServer.Assessment.Types.dll**
- This issue appears on windows server machines but the software runs on different machines and I would like to avoid temporary workarounds such as editing the registry and activate the strong name bypass feature because of the forced validation on windows server machines
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Strong name signature not valid" (#1789)

Issues.Title: Class ValueTask has different definitions between .Net Standard 2.1 and .Net 5
Issues.Body:

Issues.Title: System.Drawing.Printing.PrinterSettings slow
Issues.Body:
_This issue has been moved from [a ticket on Developer Community](https://developercommunity2.visualstudio.com/t/SystemDrawingPrintingPrinterSettings-/890524)._ --- Hello I'm debugging a problem with the printer settings. Some calls are significant slower if the default printer is a network printer, even if I explicit set a local printer name. After studying referencesource I think I found the culprit. I call: var printerSettings = new System.Drawing.Printing.PrinterSettings(); printerSettings.PrinterName = "LOCALPRINTER"; // the next call is slow if the OS default printer is a network printer var res = printerSettings.DefaultPageSettings.PrinterResolution Internally FastDeviceCapabilities is called. FastDeviceCapabilities calls GetOutputPort. But GetOutput port return the port of the default printer and not the port of the given printer! In addition, DeviceCapabilities is then called with a wrong combination of printer name and port, don't know if this could lead to additional problems. Resolution: GetOutputPort should return the port of the given printer and not accessing the default printer at all. Best Regards, Raphael --- ### Original Comments #### Raphael Affolter on 1/20/2020, 04:03 AM:

I forgot to mention: .Net Framework 4.6.1

Issues.Title: Build issues when referencing project that targets multiple frameworks C# WPF
Issues.Body:
I'm working on converting a large WPF solution's projects to SDK style and ran into some issues.

The solution is large with multiple projects(old style) all targeting .net452 and some nugets(some made by me) installed, targeting both .net452 and .netstandard2.1 This all seems to work fine, somehow the nuget manages to install the correct version targeting .net452.

I have decided to slowly convert the projects inside the solution to SDK style targeting .net452 and .netstandard2.1 just like the nugets.

This is where the problem starts, one project was converted so far that is referenced by multiple other projects. Localy everything seems to build and run fine, however when Azure DevOps(VS version 2019) is used to build the solution there are 2 scenarios:

1. The famous error message is shown:

                "Error CS0012: The type 'Object' is defined in an assembly that is not referenced. You must add a reference to assembly 
                 'netstandard, Version=2.1.0.0"

2. It builds fine but on app launch it crashes with:

                 "Could not load file or assembly 'netstandard, Version=2.1.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=cc7b13ffcd2ddd51' 
                 or one of its dependencies. The system cannot find the file specified."

I'm suspecting that the problem is related to referencing the SDK project, it looks like that somehow it references the .netstandard2.1 instead of the .net452.

The reason this is my suspicion is that if targetframework is set to only .net452 on the referenced project everything works fine. Google has led me to two possible solutions to tell the project what framework to use from the reference:

```
<ProjectReference Include="..\..\..\..\foo\foo.csproj"
                  AdditionalProperties="TargetFramework=net452">
      <Project>{xxxxxx-xxxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxxxx}</Project>
      <Name>foo</Name>
</ProjectReference>
```
and

```
<ProjectReference Include="..\..\..\..\foo\foo.csproj">
      <SetTargetFramework>TargetFramework=net452</SetTargetFramework>
      <Project>{xxxxxx-xxxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxxxx}</Project>
      <<Name>foo</Name>
</ProjectReference>
```
This doesn't look like it's doing anything and the problem still persists. At the moment I ran out of ideas and I'm here asking for help. Please let me know what I'm doing wrong or what else I can try.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Build issues when referencing project that targets multiple frameworks C# WPF" (#1776)

Issues.Body:
**TL;DR;** Requesting to add [FabricBot](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/fabricbot_overview) configuration associated with your repository to `.github/fabricbot.json`.

**Context**

FabricBot is now a [config-as-code-only](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/bot-config-as-code) platform. As a result, while you can still use the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/corefx) to modify your FabricBot configuration, you can no longer save the changes. The only way to save changes to your configuration at the moment is to _export configuration_ from the portal and upload the exported configuration to `.github/fabricbot.json` in your repository. In this pull request, we are adding your FabricBot configuration to your repository at `.github/fabricbot.json` so that you can make changes to it going forward.

While the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/corefx) is the *only way* to modify your FabricBot configuration at the moment, we have a feature on our backlog to publish the JSON schema defining the structure of the FabricBot configuration file. With the JSON schema, you can (1) use a plaintext editor of your choice to modify the FabricBot configuration file and use the schema to validate the file after editing or (2) [configure](https://code.visualstudio.com/Docs/languages/json#_json-schemas-and-settings) VS Code to use the schema when editing FabricBot configuration file to take advantage of convenience features such as automatic code completion and field description on mouseover.

[*Pull Request Create*](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/prcreate), a [MerlinBot](https://https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot) Extension, was used to automatically create this pull request. If you have any questions or concerns with this pull request, please contact [MerlinBot Expert DRI](mailto:merlinbotdri@microsoft.com).

Issues.Title: Fix RSA OAEP decryption in OpenSSL with non-power-of-two keys lengths
Issues.Body:
## Customer Impact

A customer reported in dotnet/runtime#71607 that decrypting RSA OAEP with SHA2 and a 3072-bit key on Linux resulted in a OAEP de-padding error, while other platforms were able to perform these operations successfully.

Investigation in to the issue led to uncover that RSA OAEP decryption that uses the managed implementation does not work with non-power-of-two keys because we do not slice a rented buffer accordingly. The current implementation only works because `CryptoPool.Rent` happens to give back power-of-two arrays which are exactly the same size as the key.

The fix is to slice the data to the correct size.

This does not affect dotnet/runtime because the managed implementation of RSA OAEP is no longer used for OpenSSL RSA decryption. This change was introduced in dotnet/runtime#50063.

## Testing

Unit tests were introduced to test RSA OAEP encryption with a 3072-bit RSA key. These tests will be forward-ported to dotnet/runtime.

## Risk

Minimal. The change is localized and understood that a `Slice` was missing.

Issues.Title: Update the Roslyn tests to use the editor's clipboard mock
Issues.Body:
We recently saw some failures in unit tests that were traced to the Win32 clipboard APIs being flaky. It was surprising to me that we even have code using the clipboard at all versus unit test mocks. It turns out we also have some unit tests that use the editor's IEditorOperations.Copy/Paste, which do hit the real clipboard unless we use mocks from the editor. The editor does have some mocks we could move to that were added in https://devdiv.visualstudio.com/DevDiv/_git/VSEditor/commit/a1f7e79eef29f577a027da959dc41caeb50b355e?_a=compare&path=/src/Editor/Text/Test/Integration/WpfEditor/WpfEditorTests.cs, which would help our tests stabilize.

The belief was the actual interference was coming from either the Windows clipboard history feature or the Remote Desktop clipboard helper, and isn't actually our code doing anything wrong.

Issues.Title: Add Copilot session IDs to language server telemetry
Issues.Body:
Attach the client's `COPILOT_AGENT_SESSION_ID` environment variable to each language server telemetry session as the `roslyn.languageserver.copilotSessionId` common property.

In standalone mode, `Program` reads `COPILOT_AGENT_SESSION_ID` directly from the process environment. In daemon mode, one process hosts servers for multiple clients, so the daemon's own telemetry session omits the property and each client sends its value over the named pipe before LSP traffic starts:

- `DaemonClient` writes a length-prefixed UTF-8 frame through `DaemonHandshake` right after connecting, sending length `0` when the variable is unset or whitespace and rejecting values over 1024 bytes.
- `LanguageServerConnectionManager` reads that frame per connection with a 30-second timeout before constructing `LanguageServerHost`, so a stalled client cannot block the accept loop.

Issues.Title: VB: don't report intrinsic/enum receivers of method calls as written in data flow analysis
Issues.Body:
Fixes #68286.

In VB, `AnalyzeDataFlow` reports `i` in `WrittenInside` for

```vb
Public Sub Test(i As Integer)
    Dim s = i.ToString()
End Sub
```

C# reports only `s` for the equivalent code.

`AbstractFlowPass.WriteLValueCallReceiver` treats a call on an lvalue receiver of a value type as a write to the receiver, because a structure's method can change its fields. The parameter in the issue is not written by `EnterParameter` (the suspected line): the write comes from the `ToString()` call. That reasoning doesn't apply to intrinsic and enum types: their instance methods can't change the value they are called on.

## Changes

- `WriteLValueCallReceiver` now skips the write for intrinsic and enum receivers, the same way it already does for reference types. An extension method whose first parameter is `ByRef` still counts as a write, as it does for reference types.
- User-defined structures are unchanged: calling a method on one is still a write.

## Tests

New tests in `RegionAnalysisTests.vb`:

- `MethodCallOnIntrinsicParameter_NotWrittenInside`: the case from the issue.
- `MethodCallOnIntrinsicAndEnumLocals_NotWrittenInside`: `Date`, `Decimal` and enum locals.
- `MethodCallOnStructureLocal_StillWrittenInside`: a structure method call is still a write.
- `ExtensionMethodCallOnIntrinsicLocal`: a `ByRef` extension method still writes its `Integer` receiver, while a `ByVal` one does not.

The first two fail without the fix; the last two pass with and without it.

Eleven existing assertions expected the old behavior and are updated. Each comes from a `.ToString()` call on an `Integer`, `Byte` or `Long`:

- `WrittenOutside` loses `y` in `TestIfStatementWithAssignments`, `TestIfStatementWithConstantCondition`, `TestIfStatementWithNonConstantCondition` and `TestTernaryExpressionWithAssignments` (in both `RegionAnalysisTests` and `RegionAnalysisTestsWithStaticLocals`). The C# versions of these tests already expect only `x`.
- `WrittenInside` loses `x` in `ObjectInitializersLocalsAccessed2` (both files), where the region is `.FieldInt.ToString()` on a `Long` field.
- `WrittenInside` loses `local` in `TestTryWithLambda03`, from `local.ToString()` on a `Byte`.

Local test runs (net10.0):

- `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.VisualBasic.Semantic.UnitTests`: 5508 passed, 0 failed.
- `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.VisualBasic.Emit.UnitTests`: 4236 passed, 0 failed.
- VB `ExtractMethod` and `IntroduceVariable` tests, which use region data flow: 206 passed in `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.VisualBasic.Features.UnitTests` and 491 in `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.VisualBasic.EditorFeatures.UnitTests` (net472), 0 failed.
- `dotnet format whitespace --verify-no-changes` passes on the changed files.

Issues.Title: Stop scanning preceding siblings in SyntaxNavigator.GetNextToken/GetPreviousToken
Issues.Body:
Fixes #72861.

`SyntaxNavigator` found the next or previous token by enumerating the parent's `ChildNodesAndTokens()` from the start until it reached the current token or node, then continuing from there. For a child of a long list, every `GetNextToken`/`GetPreviousToken` call is O(number of siblings), so walking all the tokens of a list is quadratic. `NormalizeWhitespace` walks tokens this way, which is why the large array initializer in the issue takes so long.

## Changes

- `SyntaxNavigator` now finds the current child's index first and only looks at the children after it (or before it, for `GetPreviousToken`). The four loops (token and node, next and previous) share two helpers, `GetFirstTokenAfterChild` and `GetLastTokenBeforeChild`.
- For a token, the index is `SyntaxToken.Index`. The old loop matched with `child.AsToken() == current`, and token equality already includes the index, so checking the child at that index gives the same result as the scan.
- For a node, the new `ChildSyntaxList.IndexOf(parent, child)` goes from the child's position to the slot that holds it, then to the list element with `FindSlotIndexContainingOffset` (a binary search for lists with many children). Zero-width children share a position with their neighbors, so it also checks the zero-width elements just before the candidate and a zero-width child at the end of a slot, and confirms the match by identity.

The results are the same as before; only the cost of locating the current child changes.

## Tests

New tests in `SyntaxNodeTests.cs`:

- `TestGetNextAndPreviousTokenWithZeroWidthListElements`: missing nodes and tokens in short and long (10+) lists, checked against `DescendantTokens()` with and without `includeZeroWidth`.
- `TestGetNextAndPreviousTokenIntoStructuredTrivia`: directives and doc comments, checked against `DescendantTokens(descendIntoTrivia: true)`.
- `TestGetNextAndPreviousTokenInLargeList`: walks every token of a 50,000-element initializer forward and backward.

The first two pass both before and after this change. The large-list test runs in under a second with the change; without it, the test run was still going when it hit a 15-minute timeout.

Issues.Title: Fix VB SyntaxFactory overloads that throw for value-carrying tokens
Issues.Body:
Fixes #69258.

`SyntaxFactory.RegionDirectiveTrivia()` throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` because the generated parameterless overload builds its `Name` with `SyntaxFactory.Token(SyntaxKind.StringLiteralToken)`, and `Token` only accepts keyword and punctuation kinds.

The VB syntax generator treats every token child except `IdentifierToken` as auto-creatable and defaults it with `SyntaxFactory.Token(kind)`. Besides `RegionDirectiveTrivia()`, that gives 12 other public overloads that always throw:

- `ExternalSourceDirectiveTrivia()`, `ExternalChecksumDirectiveTrivia()`, `ReferenceDirectiveTrivia()` (string and integer literals)
- `NumericLabel()` (integer literal)
- `XmlName()`, `XmlPrefix()`, `XmlPrefixName()`, `XmlProcessingInstruction()`, `XmlDeclarationOption(value)` (XML name)
- `XmlText()`, `XmlComment()`, `XmlCDataSection()` (XML text)

## Changes

- `RedNodeFactoryWriter.GetDefaultedFactoryParameterExpression` now gets the default token from a new `GetDefaultTokenExpression`. For the four value-carrying token kinds used by these overloads, it calls the matching token factory with an empty value: `StringLiteralToken("""""", "")`, `IntegerLiteralToken("0", ...)`, `XmlNameToken("", ...)` and `XmlTextLiteralToken("", "")`. All other kinds keep `SyntaxFactory.Token(kind)`.
- Regenerated `Syntax.xml.Main.Generated.vb` with `eng/generate-compiler-code.cmd`. Only those 13 overloads change.

No public API is added or removed, so the overloads that always threw now return a node instead. I went with this rather than making these children required in the generator, because that would remove shipped overloads. Happy to switch if you'd prefer that direction.

## Tests

Two new tests in `SyntaxFactoryTests.vb`: `RegionDirectiveTrivia_WithoutArguments`, the case from the issue, and `FactoriesWithDefaultedValueTokens_DoNotThrow`, which calls the other 12 overloads. Both fail without the regenerated file with the `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` from the issue, and pass with it.

Issues.Title: Compiler hangs when a parameter default value uses the natural type of its own method group
Issues.Body:
**Version Used**: Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp 4.8.0, 4.14.0, 5.0.0, 5.6.0, 5.9.0, 5.13.0-1.26511.1, and the compiler of the .NET SDK 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148

## Steps to Reproduce

Compile the following code:

```cs
class C
{
    void M(object a = M) { }
}
```

The compilation never completes: `dotnet build` and `Compilation.GetDiagnostics()` hang, using a CPU core.

Standalone repro with the Roslyn API:

```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp" Version="5.9.0" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
```

```cs
using Microsoft.CodeAnalysis;
using Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp;

var compilation = CSharpCompilation.Create(
    "Repro",
    [CSharpSyntaxTree.ParseText("class C { void M(object a = M) { } }")],
    [MetadataReference.CreateFromFile(typeof(object).Assembly.Location)],
    new CSharpCompilationOptions(OutputKind.DynamicallyLinkedLibrary));

var task = Task.Run(() => compilation.GetDiagnostics());
Console.WriteLine(task.Wait(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10)) ? "Completed" : "GetDiagnostics() did not complete after 10 seconds");
```

Other inputs that hang (all with `LangVersion` 10 or later):

| Input | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `class C { void M(object a = M) { } }` | Hang |
| `class C { void M(int a = M == null) { } }` | Hang |
| `class C { void M(bool a = M == M) { } }` | Hang |
| `class C { void M(int a = 0, int b = M == null) { } }` | Hang |
| `void M(int a = M == null) { }` (top-level local function) | Hang |
| `class C { void M(int a = M == null) { } }` with `LangVersion` 9 | CS0019 |
| `class C { void M(int a = M is null) { } }` | CS0837 |
| `class C { void M() { } void N(int a = M == null) { } }` | CS1736 |

The input was found by fuzzing ([meziantou/Meziantou.Analyzer#1775](https://github.com/meziantou/Meziantou.Analyzer/issues/1775)). The original input was reduced to `void value(int a = value == null) { }`.

## Expected Behavior

The compilation completes and reports an error, such as CS1736 (`Default parameter value for 'a' must be a compile-time constant`), as it does when the method group refers to another method.

## Actual Behavior

The compilation never completes. The thread waits for itself:

1. `SourceComplexParameterSymbolBase.get_DefaultSyntaxValue` binds the default value of `a`.
2. Binding `M == null` (or the conversion of `M` to `object`) asks for the natural type of the method group `M` (`FunctionTypeSymbol.GetInternalDelegateType`).
3. `Binder.GetMethodGroupOrLambdaDelegateType` reads `ParameterSymbol.HasExplicitDefaultValue` of the parameters of `M`, so it reads the default value of `a` again.
4. The default value of `a` is not complete yet, so `SymbolCompletionState.SpinWaitComplete` waits for it forever, on the thread that is computing it.

It does not hang with C# 9, as method groups have no natural type before C# 10.

Stack trace (Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp 5.9.0, trimmed):

Issues.Title: Drain compilation event queue in compiler-only analysis
Issues.Body:
### Problem

For compiler-only single-file analysis, `CompilationWithAnalyzers` reuses the root `_compilation`. Binding the file enqueues `SymbolDeclaredCompilationEvent`s on that compilation's event queue, but this path never reads the queue. The events and the semantic models they reference stay alive until the project changes.

On a large solution in the language server, a heap dump showed one project's queue holding 20,217 events.

### Fix

Drain the root compilation's event queue once the compiler-only single-file analysis completes.

A new test was also added which fails without the change (14 events left) and passes with it.

Issues.Title: [release/10.400] Check each referenced project once in dotnet format
Issues.Body:
Backport of #56621 to `release/10.0.4xx`. Fixes #56363 for .NET 10.

#56621 merged to `main` on 2026-10-28.

## Description

Before running analyzers, `dotnet format style` / `dotnet format analyzers` checks that every referenced project loaded by recursively walking `ProjectReferences`. The walk never remembers which projects it already checked, so a shared dependency is re-walked once per path that reaches it, which is exponential in the depth of the reference graph.

This replaces the recursion with a single pass over the project and its transitive dependencies from the solution's cached `ProjectDependencyGraph`, so each project is checked once.

This is a manual port, not a cherry-pick. On this branch the check is the synchronous `AllReferencedProjectsLoaded` (an `mscorlib.dll` metadata-reference check) under `src/BuiltInTools/dotnet-format`, rather than the async compilation check on `main`. The port keeps this branch's check exactly as is and changes only how the graph is walked. The test is translated from MSTest to xUnit.

## Customer Impact

On solutions with dense project-reference graphs (for example, ones using `DisableTransitiveProjectReferences`), `dotnet format style` / `analyzers` runs for minutes to hours. #56363 reports 11.5 minutes on a 30-project repro and 14+ hours on a 380-project solution. Teams that use `dotnet format --verify-no-changes` as a CI gate can't run it. The only workarounds are formatting project by project or skipping the analyzer passes.

## Regression?

No. The unmemoized walk is long-standing; it is also present in .NET 8 (`dotnet/format`).

## Risk

Low. The change is limited to the pre-analysis reference check. The set of projects checked is the same (the project plus its transitive project references), and so is the per-project check. Any dependency that fails the check still skips the project with the existing "required references did not load" warning.

## Testing

New `AnalyzerRunnerTests`: a dense 40-project graph (each project references every earlier one) completes in seconds; without the fix it effectively never finishes and the test harness's hang detection trips.

Issues.Title: Fix flaky cross-entry-point telemetry drain assertion
Issues.Body:
## Summary

Fixes #56957.

The Windows CI failure occurs at `drainerBlob.Should().NotBeNull()`: the test requires the draining command to persist its own telemetry, even though failed-command shutdown only gives the exporter a bounded 300-ms opportunity to finish. Persistence of that new payload is not guaranteed and is incidental to the cross-entry-point drain contract.

Remove the drainer-payload and directory-comparison assertions. Explicitly require the writer's telemetry to remain persisted and have a `.lock` suffix after the other entry point runs. This directly verifies that the other entry point found and leased the existing blob. Keep both managed-to-AOT and AOT-to-managed cases and the separate successful-shutdown persistence coverage. No production behavior changes.

Related: #56958 proposes the same assertion removal; this change additionally documents the bounded-shutdown rationale and explicitly checks that the writer's blob remains present.

## Validation

- Ran `scripts\RunTests.cs` for `PersistentStorageTelemetryE2ETests` with `--repeat 20`: all 80 test cases passed, with no skips or failures.
- Scoped `git diff --check` passed.
- The full repository build encountered unrelated TemplateEngine project-reference and Windows long-path errors. A redist-only build produced the managed/AOT binaries used by the focused tests, but its final overlay reported unrelated missing targeting-pack resource files.

Issues.Title: Add CA1882: Avoid value types that do not implement IEquatable<T> in records
Issues.Body:
Implements the analyzer approved in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/102593 ("Don't include non-`IEquatable` structs in records").

API review decision ([comment by bartonjs](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/102593), 2026-09-15): **Category: Performance, Severity: Info**.

## Rule

**CA1882: Avoid value types that do not implement IEquatable\<T> in records** — `Performance`, `RuleLevel.IdeSuggestion` (Info), C# only, no code fix.

The equality members the compiler generates for a record compare every instance field through `EqualityComparer<T>.Default`. For a value type that does not implement `IEquatable<T>` of itself, that resolves to `ObjectEqualityComparer<T>`, which calls `Object.Equals(Object)` and boxes on every comparison.

```csharp
public struct Point { public int X, Y; }

public record struct Line(Point Start, Point End);   // CA1882 on 'Start' and 'End'
```

CA1881 is claimed by https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/pull/56870, so this takes CA1882. Whichever PR merges second needs to re-check the range in `DiagnosticCategoryAndIdRanges.txt`.

## What is reported

The analyzer looks at the instance fields declared in a record (class or struct), because those are exactly what the generated `Equals` compares. That covers:

- positional parameters (reported on the parameter),
- auto-properties, including ones using the `field` keyword (reported on the property),
- explicitly declared fields.

A member is reported when its type — or the underlying type of `Nullable<T>` — is a struct that does not implement `IEquatable<T>` of itself.

**Scope note:** the proposal text only talks about positional parameters. Fields and auto-properties declared in the record body take part in the generated equality in exactly the same way, so they are reported too. Happy to narrow this to positional parameters if reviewers prefer the literal proposal.

## What is not reported

- Structs that implement `IEquatable<Self>` (implicitly, explicitly, or through a derived interface), record structs, primitives, enums, tuples.
- Reference types and type parameters.
- Static members, and properties without a backing field (including a positional parameter paired with a hand-written computed property).
- Records that declare `Equals(TRecord)` themselves — the compiler then generates no member-wise equality.
- Members inherited from a base record; they are reported once, on the base record.
- Non-record types.

## Deliberate limitations

- No recursion into type arguments: `(NonEquatable, int)` or `ImmutableArray<NonEquatable>` is not reported, although the element comparison boxes too.
- Structs from referenced assemblies (for example `KeyValuePair<TKey, TValue>`, or `CancellationToken` on .NET Framework/netstandard2.0) are reported even though the user cannot add `IEquatable<T>` to them. The boxing is real, and the remedy there is to declare `Equals` on the record.

## No code fix

The fix is to implement `IEquatable<T>` on a different type, which is frequently in another file, project or assembly, and requires writing equality semantics the fixer cannot infer. The rule is added to `docs/rules-with-no-code-fix.md`.

## Validation

- 36 new unit tests in `AvoidNonEquatableValueTypesInRecordsTests` pass; `EquatableAnalyzerTests` re-run as a neighbouring sanity check.
- `./build.cmd -projects src/Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.NetAnalyzers/Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.NetAnalyzers.slnx -c Debug`: 0 warnings, 0 errors.
- **dotnet/roslyn** (`8fe8ca9a`, `Roslyn.slnx`, 502 projects) via `AnalyzerRunner /a AvoidNonEquatableValueTypesInRecordsAnalyzer`: 8 diagnostics, 6 distinct after removing multi-targeting duplicates. All 6 were checked by hand and are true positives:

  | Record | Member | Struct |
  |---|---|---|
  | `NavigationBarQueueItem` (net472) | `NonFrozenComputationToken` | `CancellationToken?` |
  | `TagSourceQueueItem` (net472) | `NonFrozenComputationToken` | `CancellationToken?` |

Issues.Title: `dotnetup`: `Microsoft.Dotnet.Installation` strings are never localized
Issues.Body:
### Description

`Microsoft.Dotnet.Installation` is built into `dotnetup`, and its `Strings.resx` messages are shown to users. Unlike `dotnetup.Library`, they are never translated, so users with a non-English UI language get a mix of translated and English output.

Strings affected include:
- Archive download and extraction errors (`ArchiveDownloadFailed`, `ArchiveCorrupted`, `ArchiveExtractFailed`, `ArchiveReadPermissionDenied`, …)
- The native TAR fallback messages
- `NoUserInstallableArtifact`

### Cause

[`Microsoft.Dotnet.Installation.csproj`](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/blob/release/dnup/src/Installer/Microsoft.Dotnet.Installation/Microsoft.Dotnet.Installation.csproj) sets `<IsShipping>false</IsShipping>`. Together with `IsPackable=false`, that was added to stop the package from being published, because of an Arcade issue that broke Maestro promotion to `dotnet-tools`.

As a side effect, Arcade's `Localization.targets` only adds `Microsoft.DotNet.XliffTasks` when `IsShippingAssembly == true`. As a result:
- There are no `xlf/Strings.*.xlf` files for this project, while `dotnetup.Library` has them.
- OneLocBuild never sees these strings, so they are never translated.
- No `Microsoft.Dotnet.Installation.resources.dll` satellite assemblies are produced. Only the `dotnetup.Library.resources.dll` ones are.
- CI doesn't flag new or changed resx entries as out of date with their xlf files.

### Proposed fix

1. Set `<IsShippingAssembly>true</IsShippingAssembly>` in the project, keeping `IsShipping=false` and `IsPackable=false` so the package still isn't published. Alternatively, enable XliffTasks for this project directly.
2. Check that this has no unwanted signing or publishing side effects, and that the Maestro promotion problem doesn't come back.
3. Run `/t:UpdateXlf` and commit the generated `xlf/Strings.*.xlf` files.
4. Confirm the satellite assemblies are included in the published `dotnetup`, including the AOT/single-file layout.

### Acceptance criteria

- `src/Installer/Microsoft.Dotnet.Installation/xlf/Strings.*.xlf` exist and CI checks them.
- With a translated UI culture selected (for example `DOTNET_CLI_UI_LANGUAGE=de`), the library's messages appear in that language once translations land.
- The package is still not published.

### Related

- #55330: makes dotnetup tests localization-safe. It covers tests that check English text, not whether these strings get translated.

Issues.Title: Make ProjectAssetsFile available in cross-targeting builds
Issues.Body:
Fixes #49426.

## Change

Move the existing `ProjectAssetsFile` default and path normalization from `Microsoft.PackageDependencyResolution.targets` into `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Common.targets`, which is already imported by single-target, inner, and cross-targeting builds. The outer evaluation can now answer `dotnet restore --getProperty:ProjectAssetsFile --getProperty:TargetFrameworks` on the first clean restore, without relying on generated NuGet props that MSBuild intentionally suppresses during restore. The unmodified outer query is also empty on repeated ordinary restores, not just the first run.

This retains the existing fallback based on `MSBuildProjectExtensionsPath`, explicit/imported-property precedence, and immutable global-property behavior. The value is an expected input path, **not proof that restore ran or the file exists**. Relative project-defined paths receive the same normalization in outer builds as in inner builds. It does not import inner dependency-resolution targets into the outer build, change NuGet's output locations, or force generated props to load. Removing the established fallback entirely would be a separate contract change; that alternative remains under discussion in the review thread.

## Regression coverage

`GivenThatWeQueryProjectAssetsFile` in `Microsoft.NET.Restore.Tests` adds six single-/multi-target restore/build cases and four explicit-property evaluation cases. Coverage checks clean pre-restore evaluation (including that querying does not create the file), first and repeated restore, post-restore evaluation, inner evaluation, valid multi-property JSON, custom extensions paths, aligned `RestoreOutputPath`/`ProjectAssetsFile`, path normalization, explicit/global overrides, and build outputs for each TFM.

## Source-built CI validation

At head `462c92ff0e49460912aa9819e5e140e8150d4c15`, [build 1671535](https://dev.azure.com/dnceng-public/public/_build/results?buildId=1671535) successfully compiled all ten SDK build legs. The [Windows restore-suite TRX](https://helixr1107v0xdeko0k025g8.blob.core.windows.net/dotnet-sdk-refs-pull-57006-merge-5053d12ddee9423d8e/Microsoft.NET.Restore.Tests.dll/1/Microsoft.NET.Restore.Tests_net12.0_x64.trx?helixlogtype=result) confirms **all 10 new regressions passed against the source-built SDK**; the suite reports 46 passed, 6 not executed, and 0 failed.

The overall pipeline remains **red**, not green: its sole failure is `PersistentStorageTelemetryE2ETests.ItDrainsTelemetryPersistedByTheOtherEntryPoint(False)` on Windows, with `Expected string not to be <null>`. This matches the exact case/assertion in independent [main build 1666828](https://dev.azure.com/dnceng-public/public/_build/results?buildId=1666828), verified in its [console log](https://helixr1107v0xdeko0k025g8.blob.core.windows.net/dotnet-sdk-refs-heads-main-36c007f6f9ce4dbe9f/dotnet.Tests.dll.19/1/console.ad40f524.log?helixlogtype=result), and is tracked by #56957. No telemetry changes, blind reruns, or check bypasses are included here.

## Earlier local validation

Serial real-CLI matrices on installed SDK `10.0.300-preview.0.26177.108` reproduced the issue before the change and passed with the modified source target files overlaid into a private SDK copy: 12 baseline cases and 12 after-change cases, plus six ordinary restore/build controls per phase. The overlay used the modified source target files with only the task-assembly TFM adjusted from `net12.0` to the installed `net10.0` toolset; this was **target-source overlay validation, not a local compiled main/redist run**. Restore still reported `ImportProjectExtensionProps=false`.

Negative controls confirmed the pre-existing distinction between `RestoreOutputPath` (NuGet output) and `ProjectAssetsFile` (SDK input): setting only one does not relocate the other; this PR does not change that contract. The local repository runner could not start because this worktree lacks the required .NET 12 bootstrap SDK/redist; the source-built CI regression results above now supply the previously pending execution evidence.

Issues.Title: Strengthen Native AOT managed fallback integration test
Issues.Body:
## Summary

The existing fallback test invokes `build --help`, which renders natively, and accepts both successful and failing exit codes. It therefore passes even when the managed CLI is unavailable.

- Build a minimal SDK-free MSBuild project with `--no-restore` instead of requesting help.
- Require exit code 0 and a target-generated `AOT_MANAGED_FALLBACK:Core` marker to verify successful managed MSBuild execution.
- Clean up the temporary project in a `finally` block.

Related to dotnet/sdk#56404; this PR contains only the test fix and does not depend on its runner changes.

## Validation

- Fresh Native AOT publishes of `dotnet-aot` and `dn` for Windows x64 succeeded.
- Three focused integration/parser tests passed, with no skips, through `scripts/RunTests.cs`. The managed test runner drove the native host/library against an isolated copy of the bootstrap SDK.
- Negative control: temporarily removing the staged managed `dotnet.dll` left the original `build --help` invocation succeeding, while the strengthened test correctly failed on exit code 1. Restoring it returned the focused tests to green.
- Full redist/native-published test suite and other platforms were not rerun.

Issues.Title: Reconcile MTP vendored sources and triage team notifications
Issues.Body:
## Summary

The SDK's vendored Microsoft.Testing.Platform sources have drifted from upstream, including a changed default for captured test output. Reconcile all 16 open vendored-sync reports while preserving SDK-owned retry accounting, aggregate exit-code policies, and compatibility with older test applications.

- Default captured stdout and stderr to failed tests only in every environment, including `--output detailed`. Independent per-module `all`/`failed`/`none` overrides honor effective arguments, response files, launch profiles, and configuration. `--show-stdout all --show-stderr all` restores the previous output behavior; capture, raw process output, result visibility, counts, and exit policies are unchanged.
- Refresh all reported upstream baselines using verified blob identities at `b3f3c980c480c5d97976d658ac367b1e246502be`. Append tracking for the two new progress-state partials without reordering existing source indices or restructuring the SDK fork. Already-aligned coverage wire constants and SDK `nint` interop are retained.
- Update SDK-owned platform-option help so older test-application metadata cannot advertise the wrong default. Regenerate localization catalogs and the help snapshot, and update contributor guidance.

This branch also contains the previously committed triage fix: explicitly allow CODEOWNERS team mentions and use the correct `dotnet-testing` team snapshot. The validated agentic-workflow upgrade is included in a separate commit, with its scope and validation described below.

## Agentic workflow upgrade

Resolve the tooling upgrade notice by adopting gh-aw v1.0.1 and refreshing pinned actions, containers, and all ten generated runtime workflows. Preserve strict sandboxing and existing workflow safety boundaries while migrating the compiler's changed interfaces.

- Move completion checks out of unsupported conclusion hooks, preserve visible incomplete-triage failures with isolated grading, and keep CI issue dispatch tied to the trusted creation-map artifact.
- Queue frozen source interpretations through the normal native safe-output API. The agent forwards only the validated receipt; trusted code supplies the full payload without agent-side serialization or post-step safe-output rewrites. Confirmed repeats reuse the acknowledgement, and unconfirmed requests are not retried.
- Preserve the 512 KiB submission budget and explicitly grant the reusable interpreter's caller the compiler-required `pull-requests: read` scope. Triage uses the SDK-mode proxy-aware fetch tool because native offline CLI web tools are unavailable.

Validation of this separate upgrade: all ten workflows compile with gh-aw v1.0.1; 74 focused regressions pass; and the shipping v0.5.0 gateway composed with the actual trusted client passes recording at the full 512 KiB limit, authentication, and receipt-rejection checks. Hosted interpreter execution was not run.

## Validation of the reconciliation

- Managed CLI and complete Debug SDK layout builds succeeded, including Native AOT publication.
- Focused SDK regressions passed: 270 tests, zero failures or skips, including real packaged MTP output and invalid-option diagnostics.
- Five actual Native AOT SDK muxer scenarios on Windows x64 confirmed native execution, independent stream policies, all three test outcomes/counts, and the expected exit code.
- A buildable comparison with failed-only filtering disabled produced three intended assertion failures across 11 cases. Restored source passed all 270 tests again.
- All 53 tracked upstream blobs match the verified snapshot; source indices, regenerated localization states, and affected documentation links were checked.

Issues.Title: dotnet watch launched by Aspire passes the entire environment as dotnet run -e KEY=VALUE arguments, exposing secrets in process command lines
Issues.Body:
### Describe the bug

When an Aspire AppHost is started with `aspire run` (hot reload / watch mode), each project resource is started through `dotnet watch`, which in turn launches the app as:

```
dotnet run --no-build -e KEY1=VALUE1 -e KEY2=VALUE2 … (150–180 pairs)
```

The `-e` list contains the **complete inherited environment** of the user session, including variables that hold credentials (API keys, access tokens, client secrets). Process command lines are readable by any local process (Task Manager, `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process`, `ps`), and are commonly recorded by EDR/Defender, process-creation auditing (Event ID 4688) and crash/diagnostic tooling. Environment variables of a process are not exposed this way, so materialising them as arguments turns a private value into a widely visible one.

### Observed process chain (Windows 11)

```
aspire.exe
 └─ dotnet watch --non-interactive --project <Project>.csproj        (no -e arguments)
     └─ dotnet …/dotnet-watch.dll …
         └─ dotnet run --no-build -e … -e …   (≈150–180 -e pairs = full environment)
```

Plain `dotnet watch` outside of Aspire does **not** show this: in a minimal console project, the child `dotnet run` received only 5 `-e` pairs (watch's own variables) and none of the inherited environment, including a test variable set on the parent. So the full list appears to come from the environment Aspire hands to `dotnet watch` for the resource, which `dotnet watch` then materialises as `-e` arguments.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Set a dummy user environment variable, e.g. `REPRO_FAKE_SECRET=not-a-real-secret`.
2. Create an Aspire AppHost with one project resource (e.g. `aspire new` starter).
3. Run `aspire run` (watch/hot reload enabled, default).
4. Inspect the command line of the project's `dotnet run` process, e.g. PowerShell:
   `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='dotnet.exe'" | ? CommandLine -match ' run --no-build -e ' | % CommandLine`

### Expected behavior

Environment variables for the launched app are passed via the child process environment (e.g. `ProcessStartInfo.Environment`), not as command-line arguments. At minimum, inherited variables that the parent already has should not be re-materialised as `-e` arguments.

### Actual behavior

All inherited variables, including secrets, appear verbatim in the `dotnet run` command line.

### Versions

- .NET SDK 10.0.302 (`dotnet-watch` 10.0.302)
- Aspire CLI 13.6.4
- Windows 11 (10.0.26300)

### Notes

Not sure whether the fix belongs in `dotnet-watch` (how it forwards the environment it receives to `dotnet run`) or in Aspire (which environment it passes to `dotnet watch`). Filing here because the materialisation as `-e` arguments happens in `dotnet-watch`; happy to move/cross-post to dotnet/aspire.

Issues.Title: Distinguish current and recommended access modes in dotnetup init
Issues.Body:
`dotnetup init` previously labeled the configured access mode as the default, obscuring the platform recommendation during reconfiguration.

- **Defaults**
  - Track the configured and platform-recommended modes separately.
  - Keep the configured mode preselected.
  - Fall back to the recommendation when the configured mode is unsupported.

- **Form**
  - Label configured modes `(current)` and platform defaults `(recommended)`.
  - Combine matching modes as `(current, recommended)`.
  - Compare change highlighting against the preselected current mode.

Example:

```text
None   (current)
Shell  (recommended)
```

- **Coverage**
  - Cover distinct, matching, and first-run labels.
  - Verify changes are measured against the current mode.

Issues.Title: .NET October 2026 out-of-band security updates
Issues.Body:
On October 25, 2026, we released out-of-band security updates for .NET 8.0.33, .NET 9.0.22, .NET 10.0.14, and .NET 11 Release Candidate 3 (prerelease). We recommend updating affected applications and build environments as soon as possible. .NET Framework is not affected.

## Release Notes

* [.NET 9.0.22 and .NET SDK 9.0.123 / 9.0.320](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/9.0/9.0.22/9.0.22.md) ([Download](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/9.0))
* [.NET 10.0.14 and .NET SDK 10.0.114 / 10.0.403](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/10.0/10.0.14/10.0.14.md) ([Download](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/10.0))
* [.NET 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 and .NET SDK 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 (prerelease)](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/11.0/preview/rc3/11.0.0-rc.3.md) ([Download](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/11.0))

## Security advisories

| Advisory | Applicability | Announcement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [CVE-2026-111497](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/security/advisories/GHSA-p3jp-9v83-76w9) | Brotli decoder out-of-bounds write; all platforms when processing untrusted Brotli data. | [Announcement](https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/494) |
| [CVE-2026-114148](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/security/advisories/GHSA-r6pf-x897-gm86) | Linux archive ownership; distribution-specific ASP.NET Core archives and source-build engineering inputs. | [Announcement](https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/495) |
| [CVE-2026-70197](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/security/advisories/GHSA-4mpw-cpwj-hxxj) | Windows sockets memory corruption; corrected October 13 fix. | [Announcement](https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/493) |
| [CVE-2026-102870](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/security/advisories/GHSA-g27p-qf6j-c96c) | Standalone Blazor WebAssembly debugger packages on .NET 10/11; corrected October 13 fix. | [Announcement](https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/492) |

The October 13 updates did not fully address CVE-2026-70197 and CVE-2026-102870. These out-of-band updates provide the corrected fixes; the original advisory identities and revision history are preserved. For CVE-2026-102870, update the affected standalone Server/DevServer package references; updating only the shared runtime is not a substitute.

For CVE-2026-114148, affected Microsoft-published .NET 8/9 ASP.NET Core runtime and targeting-pack tarball installations require a clean replacement following the advisory. Source-built archives are build/engineering inputs, not directly deployed production runtimes. Update those inputs and recreate their extracted workspaces using ownership-controlled extraction; review and rebuild affected downstream outputs as needed. .NET 10/11 applicability is limited to source-built distributions.

Also announced at [.NET October 2026 Out-of-Band Security Updates](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/dotnet-october-2026-oob-security-updates/).

Please use the [release feedback issue](https://github.com/dotnet/core/issues/10660) for release-wide issues and the linked per-CVE discussions for advisory questions.

Issues.Title: Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-114148 | .NET Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability
Issues.Body: ## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in file ownership in Linux .NET tarball distributions, including ASP.NET Core runtime tarballs, ASP.NET Core targeting-pack tarballs, and source-built .NET tarballs. This advisory also provides guidance on updating affected installations and source-build engineering workflows. Incorrect ownership of runtime files installed from affected Linux tarballs can allow local elevation of privilege. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/discussions/70040 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 7.8 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-276 (Incorrect Default Permissions) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Linux - **Architectures:** ARM, ARM64 and x64, as applicable to the affected Linux distribution. ## Affected Products The affected ASP.NET Core runtime, ASP.NET Core targeting-pack, and source-built .NET Linux tarballs are listed below. The installation and source-build engineering scenarios require different remediation, as described in [How do I fix the issue?](#how-fix). ### Microsoft-published ASP.NET Core archives For Microsoft-published .NET 8 and .NET 9 distributions, only the ASP.NET Core runtime and targeting-pack tarballs are affected. Other Microsoft-published .NET runtime and SDK tarballs are not included in this scope. Product | Affected version | Patched version ------- | ---------------- | --------------- ASP.NET Core 8 regular and composite Linux runtime tarballs | >= 8.0.0, < 8.0.33 | 8.0.33 ASP.NET Core 8 Linux targeting-pack tarballs | >= 8.0.0, < 8.0.33 | 8.0.33 ASP.NET Core 9 regular and composite Linux runtime tarballs | >= 9.0.0, < 9.0.22 | 9.0.22 ASP.NET Core 9 Linux targeting-pack tarballs | >= 9.0.0, < 9.0.22 | 9.0.22 These products use the archive names `aspnetcore-runtime-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, `aspnetcore-runtime-composite-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, and `aspnetcore-targeting-pack-{version}-{rid}.tar.gz`, where `{rid}` is `linux-arm`, `linux-arm64`, `linux-x64`, `linux-musl-arm`, `linux-musl-arm64` or `linux-musl-x64`. Runtime tarballs are listed on the [.NET download site](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet); targeting-pack tarballs are distributed through the .NET download CDN. ### Source-built distributions Every tarball type produced by source-build is affected in the ranges below, not only SDK tarballs. The versions in this table identify the corresponding source-build SDK release. Source-built tarballs are used in build and engineering workflows, rather than deployed directly to customer installations. Consuming an affected source-build archive does not, by itself, mean that a production shared runtime was installed from that archive. Product | Affected version | Patched version ------- | ---------------- | --------------- Source-built .NET 8 Linux distributions | >= 8.0.100, < 8.0.133 | 8.0.133 Source-built .NET 9 Linux distributions | >= 9.0.100, < 9.0.123 | 9.0.123 Source-built .NET 10.0.1xx Linux distributions | >= 10.0.100, <= 10.0.113 | 10.0.114-servicing.26522.126 Source-built .NET 10.0.4xx Linux distributions | >= 10.0.400, <= 10.0.402 | 10.0.403-servicing.26523.112 Source-built .NET 11 preview Linux distributions | >= 11.0.100-preview.1.26104.118, <= 11.0.100-rc.2.26504.105 | 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? Review whether an installation came from an affected ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack tarball, or whether a build or engineering workflow consumes an affected source-built archive. Check whether extraction preserved numeric ownership and whether the resulting files have the intended ownership. A .NET version number alone does not identify which archive was used or establish the ownership of an installation or build workspace. The vulnerability can affect installations that preserve numeric file ownership from an affected archive, for example during privileged extraction or ownership-preserving container archive import. A local account that controls the installed files or writable directories may be able to modify files used by a more privileged application. Restoring ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack NuGet packages does not, by itself, introduce this tarball ownership defect. Applications using a shared runtime installed from an affected tarball can still be affected. ### How do I fix the issue? #### Customer-deployed installations For an installation made from an affected ASP.NET Core runtime or targeting-pack tarball, replace the affected installation with a clean installation from the patched distribution listed in [Affected Products](#affected-products). Updating a NuGet reference, downloading a new archive, or extracting over an existing installation does not by itself correct the existing installation. 1. Identify the affected installation directories and the applications, services, scheduled jobs, and container images that use them. Stop affected applications and services before switching installations. 2. Obtain the patched archives appropriate to your distribution, architecture, and required components from the trusted publisher. Verify their checksums against the publisher's trusted release information before extracting them. 3. Install into a **new, empty directory**, not the affected installation tree. For a shared or privileged installation, use a trusted administrator account and an administrator-controlled directory whose parent directories cannot be modified by untrusted accounts. Do not copy binaries, plugins, or other files from the affected tree into the replacement. Install any required side-by-side versions from trusted, fixed distributions. 4. Extract without restoring the archive's user/group ownership. Follow the [manual installation guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/install/linux-scripted-manual#manual-install), which uses `--no-same-owner`. For GNU tar, the following example also applies a restrictive write-permission mask: ```bash ( umask 022 tar -xzf "$PATCHED_ARCHIVE" -C "$NEW_DOTNET_ROOT" \ --no-same-owner --no-same-permissions ) ``` `PATCHED_ARCHIVE` must identify the verified patched archive, and `NEW_DOTNET_ROOT` must identify the new, empty installation directory. For a shared or privileged installation, run extraction in the trusted administrator context. Confirm that the resulting files, directories, and parent directories are controlled by the intended trusted owner and cannot be modified by untrusted accounts, including through group permissions or access-control lists. 5. Update application and service configuration to use the replacement installation, then restart and verify the applications. Check the actual runtime selected by each application, not only the version reported by an unrelated `dotnet` executable on `PATH`. Ensure that no service, scheduled job, or runtime search path still selects the affected installation. Retire the old tree using your deployment procedures, preserving evidence first if compromise is suspected. 6. Rebuild affected custom container images from trusted inputs using the patched archives and ownership-controlled extraction, and deploy replacement containers. Changing only a running container does not correct the image used to create subsequent containers. #### Source-build engineering workflows If a build or engineering workflow consumes an affected source-built tarball, update that input to the patched source-build release listed in [Affected Products](#affected-products). Recreate its extracted workspace in a new, trusted directory using ownership-controlled extraction, rather than reusing a tree extracted from the affected archive. The extraction guidance above also applies to these workspaces. Review downstream runtime or SDK packages and custom images for ownership inherited from the affected archive, and rebuild affected outputs as needed. The customer-installation steps above apply if affected outputs were actually installed or deployed; do not treat the source-build engineering archive itself as a deployed production runtime. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). Further information can be found in the MSRC [Report an Issue FAQ](https://www.microsoft.com/msrc/faqs-report-an-issue). Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty. ### Support You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue. ### Disclaimer The information provided in this advisory is provided "as is" without warranty of any kind. Microsoft disclaims all warranties, either express or implied, including the warranties of merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose. In no event shall Microsoft Corporation or its suppliers be liable for any damages whatsoever including direct, indirect, incidental, consequential, loss of business profits or special damages, even if Microsoft Corporation or its suppliers have been advised of the possibility of such damages. Some states do not allow the exclusion or limitation of liability for consequential or incidental damages so the foregoing limitation may not apply. ### External Links [CVE-2026-114148](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-114148) ### Acknowledgements - Alen Cheung ### Revisions V1.0 (10/25/2026): Initial advisory.

Issues.Title: Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-111497 | .NET Brotli Decoder Out-of-bounds Write Vulnerability
Issues.Body: ## Executive summary A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege. ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/136446 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.1 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** All - **Architectures:** All ## Mitigations ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths: - Enable ASP.NET Core [automatic request decompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/request-decompression) with Brotli (`br`) support. - Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring [HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.httpclienthandler.automaticdecompression) or [SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.socketshttphandler.automaticdecompression) to include [DecompressionMethods.Brotli](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.decompressionmethods) or `DecompressionMethods.All`. - Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in `System.IO.Compression`, such as `BrotliStream` or `BrotliDecoder`. Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data. The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it. > **Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression.** Do not introduce a call to `AddRequestDecompression` if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an `AutomaticDecompression` property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded. If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the `br` entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers: ```csharp builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options => { options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br"); }); ``` If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include `DecompressionMethods.Brotli`: ```csharp var handler = new HttpClientHandler { AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate }; var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler); ``` Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix. ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT packages Issues.Title: Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-70197 | .NET and Visual Studio Remote Code Execution Vulnerability | October 25, 2026 OOB update
Issues.Body: ## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in System.Net.Sockets. This advisory also provides guidance on what developers can do to update their applications to remove this vulnerability. On Windows, reusing a `SocketAsyncEventArgs` instance across IPv4 and IPv6 datagram sockets can retain an undersized cached native address buffer, allowing an unauthenticated out-of-bounds write during `ReceiveFromAsync`. This vulnerability was disclosed in the October 13 advisory, but the fix was not included in the previous updates. This revision provides the corrected packages under the existing CVE-2026-70197. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/136445 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.1 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Windows - **Architectures:** All ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects Microsoft .NET projects that use an affected package version listed below. If using a package listed in [affected packages](#affected-packages), you're exposed to the vulnerability. The affected .NET 8 Windows packages include both CoreCLR and Mono runtime packs. The issue requires reuse of `SocketAsyncEventArgs` across IPv4 and IPv6 datagram sockets; it is not limited to one runtime implementation. ### How do I fix the issue? 1. To fix the issue please install the latest version of .NET. If you have installed one or more .NET SDKs through Visual Studio, Visual Studio will prompt you to update Visual Studio, which will also update your .NET SDKs. 2. If your application references the vulnerable package, update the package reference to the patched version. You can list the versions you have installed by running the `dotnet --info` command. * If you're using .NET 8.0, you should download and install .NET 8.0.33 Runtime or .NET 8.0.133 or 8.0.427 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/8.0. * If you're using .NET 9.0, you should download and install .NET 9.0.22 Runtime or .NET 9.0.123 or 9.0.320 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/9.0. * If you're using .NET 10.0, you should download and install .NET 10.0.14 Runtime or .NET 10.0.114 or 10.0.403 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/10.0. * If you're using .NET 11.0, you should download and install .NET 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148 Runtime or .NET 11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/11.0.
